say.text: A 58-year-old woman has a thickened area in one breast that does not feel like a clear lump. Biopsy shows small, uniform cells lined up one behind another. Mammography shows no mass.
Which type is this?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ignore which type is commonest. Ask how the cells sit: glands in a firm mass, or one behind another?
That is not the right choice. Ductal is the commonest type, so it feels like the default answer to every type question.
But ductal cancer usually forms one hard, stellate mass, and this biopsy shows a line of cells with no mass. Commonest is not the same as fits the picture.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so note it: a common type is not the answer to a question about spread.

say.text: That is not the right choice. Medullary is a real type, but it does not fit single-file cells.
Medullary is soft and well defined, with a lymphocytic infiltrate, so it forms a clear mass.
Yes. Lobular cells grow in single file because E-cadherin is lost, so they spread through the breast without forming one mass.
That is also why lobular is more often bilateral and multicentric.
Yes. Ductal is the commonest type: a hard, gritty, stellate mass, the scirrhous picture.
Lobular cells lie in single file with loss of E-cadherin. They are often bilateral and multicentric, and spread to peritoneum, ovaries and meninges.
Commonest and bilateral are different questions. Luminal A is the most common molecular subtype.
Years after a breast cancer, a woman has deposits in the peritoneum and ovaries, and a tumour in the other breast.
Which primary type is most likely?
That is not the right choice. The scirrhous ductal mass is the picture most people hold for breast cancer, so it becomes the default.
Spread to the peritoneum and ovaries, with the other breast involved, is the lobular pattern.
That is not the right choice. Medullary is soft and well defined, and it is not known for this pattern of spread.
Medullary carcinoma has a lymphocytic infiltrate and a clear edge, which does not explain peritoneal and ovarian deposits.
Yes. Peritoneal and ovarian deposits with a bilateral picture are the lobular pattern.
BRCA1 and BRCA2 are two separate breast cancer genes, each on its own chromosome arm.
Which pairing of gene and arm is right?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Each gene has its own arm. Do not learn the two numbers as one unordered pair.
That is not the right choice. The numbers 13 and 17 come as a pair, so it is easy to swap which gene owns which.
The exam tests the gene-to-arm link, so each gene needs its own fact.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so fix the swap: the pair of numbers is not the fact to remember.

say.text: Yes. BRCA1 is on 17q and BRCA2 on 13q.
A breast and ovarian cancer family has a mutation on chromosome 17q.
Which gene is it?
That is not the right choice. Two numbers that go together are easy to swap, so 17q slides to the wrong gene.
Here the arm is the clue: attach each arm to its own gene, not to a number pair.
Yes. BRCA1 is on 17q, so a 17q mutation in a breast and ovarian family points to BRCA1.
Male breast cancer is rare. Which gene is it most linked to?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Pick by the phenotype a man with breast cancer shows, not by which gene you know best.
That is not the right choice. BRCA1 is the best-known breast gene, so it becomes the default for any hereditary question.
BRCA1 cancers are typically triple-negative, a different pattern from breast cancer in a man.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the phenotype before the famous gene: male breast cancer is not the triple-negative pattern.

say.text: That is not the right choice. PTEN is a real cancer gene, but it belongs to a different hereditary syndrome.
PTEN goes with Cowden syndrome, and it is not the gene linked to male breast cancer.
Yes. BRCA2 is the gene more tied to male breast cancer, along with Klinefelter syndrome.
BRCA1 cancers are typically triple-negative, the basal-like pattern.
BRCA2 is the gene more tied to male breast cancer, which is about 1% of all breast cancers.
Match the gene to the phenotype in the stem, not to the gene you know best.
Family A has triple-negative breast cancers in several women. Family B has breast cancer in a man.
Which pairing is most likely?
That is not the right choice. BRCA1 is the gene you reach for first, so it tempts you to label both families with it.
Triple-negative women and a man with breast cancer are different phenotypes, so one gene cannot fit both.
That is not the right choice. BRCA2 fits family B, the man, but not family A.
Triple-negative cancers in several women are the BRCA1 pattern, so one gene for both families cannot work.
Yes. Triple-negative cancers in women fit BRCA1, and breast cancer in a man fits BRCA2.
A 3 cm tumour has skin over it that looks like orange peel.
What causes this skin change?

choices.label: Inflamed skin, so it means inflammatory carcinoma
Blocked subdermal lymphatics, so the skin swells
Cooper's ligaments pulling the skin inward
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Think about what drains fluid out of the skin, not about redness or heat.
That is not the right choice. Orange peel looks like the skin of inflammatory cancer, so the sign and the syndrome get merged.
One skin sign is not the whole picture. Ask what the skin's drainage does, not whether the skin is red.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the mechanism first: a single sign does not make a syndrome.

say.text: That is not the right choice. Cooper's ligaments do change the skin, but the change is a dimple, not orange peel.
Cooper's ligament involvement causes dimpling, which is a different sign.
Yes. Blocked subdermal lymphatics cause skin oedema, which gives the orange-peel look.
Breast A: skin dimpled over a lump, nipple normal. Breast B: orange-peel skin over a lump.
Which breast shows the lymphatic-block sign?

choices.label: Breast B: lymphatic oedema of the skin
Breast A: dimpling from Cooper's ligaments

say.text: That is not the right choice. Any skin change over a lump can tempt you to read it as the inflammatory syndrome.
A single skin sign is not the whole picture of inflammatory cancer.
That is not the right choice. Dimpling is a real skin sign, but it has a different cause from orange-peel oedema.
Dimpling comes from Cooper's ligament traction, not from blocked lymphatics.
Yes. Blocked lymphatics give oedema and orange-peel skin, while Cooper's ligament pull gives dimpling.
One thing before the genes. ER or PR positive, HER2 negative, with low Ki-67, is Luminal A, the most common molecular subtype.
That is not the right choice. 11q only looks familiar from the list of numbers you have seen.
Check each gene against its own arm: BRCA1 is on 17q and BRCA2 on 13q.
Pin each number to its gene: BRCA1 sits on 17q, BRCA2 on 13q. Say each gene with its own arm, never the pair alone.
That is not the right choice. TP53 is a real hereditary breast cancer gene, so it sounds plausible for a family history.
But TP53 is the Li-Fraumeni gene. A breast and ovarian family with a 17q mutation is the BRCA1 picture.
That is not the right choice. ATM is a known cancer-risk gene, so it can pass for a hereditary answer.
But ATM goes with ataxia-telangiectasia. The 17q arm in a breast and ovarian family points to BRCA1.
BRCA1 cancers are typically triple-negative. BRCA2 is the gene more tied to male breast cancer, which is about 1% of all breast cancers.
Blocked subdermal lymphatics cause skin oedema, which gives orange peel. Inflammatory cancer is a whole-breast syndrome, so one skin sign does not make it.
Ductal and lobular cancer look and spread differently.
Which pairing is right?

choices.label: Ductal: one hard stellate mass; lobular: single-file cells, E-cadherin lost
Ductal: single-file cells; lobular: one hard stellate mass
Both form one hard mass; ductal is just the commoner
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Think about how each type lays its cells down, and which one is known for E-cadherin loss.
That is not the right choice. The two pictures are swapped.
The hard, gritty, stellate mass is ductal. Single-file cells with E-cadherin loss are lobular.
That is not the right choice. Ductal is the commonest, so it is easy to let lobular borrow its picture.
Lobular lacks E-cadherin, grows in single file and often forms no mass, so it behaves differently from ductal.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so remember that commonest does not mean the same behaviour.

say.text: That is not the right choice. This pairing is reversed.
Triple-negative cancers in women fit BRCA1, and breast cancer in a man fits BRCA2. Here each gene is placed on the wrong family.

cards.q: Which breast cancer type is more often bilateral and multicentric?
cards.a: Invasive lobular carcinoma, with single-file cells and E-cadherin loss.

cards.q: Which BRCA gene is linked to male breast cancer, and which to triple-negative tumours?
cards.a: BRCA2 for male breast cancer; BRCA1 for triple-negative.

cards.q: What causes peau d'orange over a tumour?
cards.a: Blocked subdermal lymphatics causing skin oedema; Cooper's ligament pull gives dimpling.
